title: Explaining a new antidepressant
candidateBrief: You are a junior doctor in general practice. Priya Shah, 38, was diagnosed with a moderate depressive episode two weeks ago and has been on the waiting list for talking therapy. She has returned to discuss starting sertraline, which your senior has suggested. Explain the medication and address her concerns. You do not need to take a full history. There is no risk to self (already assessed).

patient.name: Priya Shah
patient.openingStatement: The other doctor mentioned tablets last time. I've been thinking about it, but I'm really not sure.
patient.demeanour: Thoughtful, a little tearful at times, cautious. Asks direct questions and appreciates honesty. Becomes more reassured if her worries are explored rather than dismissed.
patient.speechStyle: Clear everyday English. Asks follow-up questions. Knows some drug names from work but not how they work.

ice.ideas: Thinks antidepressants might 'change her personality' or make her feel numb.
ice.concerns: Worried about getting addicted, gaining weight, and what people at work would think.
ice.expectations: Wants honest information so she can decide herself; would prefer to avoid tablets if possible.

freelyShared: Has been feeling low for about three months and struggling to get through the day.
Is on the waiting list for talking therapy, which is about 8 weeks.

revealOnlyIfAsked.trigger: her worries or concerns about the medication
revealOnlyIfAsked.answer: My biggest worry is getting hooked on them and never being able to come off.
keywords: never being able to come off

revealOnlyIfAsked.trigger: what she has heard about antidepressants or what she thinks they do
revealOnlyIfAsked.answer: My friend said they made her feel like a zombie. I don't want to stop feeling things.

revealOnlyIfAsked.trigger: other medications, health conditions, pregnancy plans, contraception
revealOnlyIfAsked.answer: I take ibuprofen quite a lot for back pain. I have the coil, so no pregnancy plans.
Just a glass of wine at the weekend. Would I have to stop that?
keywords: glass of wine at the weekend

revealOnlyIfAsked.trigger: work or what others would think
revealOnlyIfAsked.answer: I work in a pharmacy, so I'd be picking up my own prescription in front of colleagues. That's embarrassing.

patient.cue: What would you do if you were me?

postEncounterQuestions.q: List the key points you should cover when starting an SSRI.
postEncounterQuestions.modelAnswer: How it works in simple terms; takes 2–4 weeks for benefit; common early side effects (nausea, GI upset, headache, anxiety, sleep change, sexual dysfunction) often settle; not addictive but should not be stopped abruptly (discontinuation symptoms); continue at least 6 months after feeling better; increased risk of GI bleeding with NSAIDs; early review within 1–2 weeks; safety-netting for worsening mood or suicidal thoughts, particularly early on.
keyPoints: Not addictive but don't stop abruptly

items.text: Introduces self and establishes the purpose of the consultation
Explores what she already knows and her concerns before giving information
items.evidenceHint: what do you know, any worries

items.text: Explains what the medicine is and how it helps, in plain language
Explains it takes a few weeks to work
Explains common side effects and that they often settle
Addresses addiction concern accurately (not addictive, but taper when stopping)
Checks other medications and identifies the ibuprofen interaction

items.evidenceHint: if worse, review in two weeks

items.text: Respects her choice, offers alternatives (therapy, self-help) and supports shared decision-making
Checks understanding and invites questions (avoids jargon)
